extracted.intended_audience: writers, essayists, and advertisers interested in prose style, rhetoric, and public communications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing clear, effective public prose (essays, advertisements, and general exposition), emphasizing economy, understandability, and appropriate rhetorical tone. Covers anti-patterns of obscurantism and practical advice for advertising copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of means / seek the shortest way from purpose to effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Not to use more instruments where fewer will be sufficient; to find the nearest way from truth to truth, or from purpose to effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the simplest adequate method of expression or argument; avoid unnecessary apparatus or ornament that does not further the point. Examples/anti-patterns: 'to tell the clock by algebra' or 'to drink tea by stratagem'—doing common things by needlessly complex means is a sign of misguided genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to be understood, not to be admired
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man speaks and writes with intent to be understood; when an author seeks admiration rather than comprehension he transfers his consideration from words to sounds and becomes less intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity and intelligibility over ornate phrasing or the pursuit of rhetorical effect. The moment a writer aims primarily to impress, readability suffers and the audience loses the ideas being conveyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the principal counterproductive author-styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Several species of authors counteract their purpose: the man of exuberance and copiousness; the ponderous dictator of sentences; the liberal illustrator; and the stately son of demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not: (a) diffuse thought across excessive diversities of expression (exuberance/copiousness); (b) present ideas as unwieldy lumps that are heavy but of little use (ponderous diction); (c) over-illustrate what was already clear (liberal illustrator); (d) prove with unnecessary mathematical formality what no one questions (over-formal demonstration). These are explicit anti-patterns; aim instead for proportion, concision, and relevance of example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'terrifick' or 'bugbear' style that obscures plain truths
rubrics_metrics.description: A style that so disguises evident truths and familiar propositions that they cannot be perceived; its chief intention is to terrify and amaze rather than inform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from scholastic jargon, strained definitions, and convoluted explanations that mask simplicity (illustrated by the parody of abstruse rephrasings of 'two and two make four' and quoted passages from 'Letters concerning Mind'). If readers must 'stay till the conclusion' to find the original plain truth, the style has failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain language instead of scholastic or obscure terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain language conveys clear propositions where elaborate scholastic reformulations only frighten the reader away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When simple expressions suffice, do not replace them with abstruse technicalizing. The example contrasts a child's understanding of 'two and two make four' with philosophical paraphrase that only obscures the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius in public writing is invention, but invention should serve clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is shown by invention — e.g., discovering new ways to attract attention — but invention should be subordinate to informing or serving the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovative techniques (for instance, novel advertisement formats) are valuable when they effectively communicate. Do not invent for invention's sake if it sacrifices the reader's understanding or manipulates without reasonable cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise boldly in advertisements (but beware of dishonesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Promise, large promise, is the soul of an advertisement; extravagant claims attract attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bold claims can be an effective tactic to gain notice (examples: wash-ball, exceptional duvets). However, the writer should balance attraction with credibility — hyperbole may work but risks misleading readers and diminishes long-term trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modest sincerity can be persuasive in advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Some advertisers succeed by modest sincerity — admitting limitations can increase credibility (example: a seller candidly stating a lotion will not restore youth to a fifty-year-old).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider acknowledging limits of a product rather than overpromising; modesty can appeal to refined judgment and avoid the backlash of implausible claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wanton manipulation of passions and indecent associations in ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers should avoid playing wantonly with public passions or placing noble objects beside trivial goods so as to make the noble ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about juxtaposition and emotional manipulation: placing elevated subjects next to trivial, bawdy, or comic advertisements (e.g., a majestic spectacle immediately followed by 'a fresh parcel of Dublin butter') can degrade both. Do not exploit passions irresponsibly (e.g., playing on maternal fear about infants to coerce purchase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use asperity or public censure in advertising content
rubrics_metrics.description: An advertiser may speak well of himself but ought not to exclude or censor his neighbour; asperity of language is improper without adequate provocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid aggressive, disparaging attacks on competitors in public notices (examples: disputes about straps for razors or eau de luce). Maintain civility and focus on one's own merits rather than attempting to debase others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisers should write with dignity and consider posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers of advertisements should remember their name stands alongside eminent persons in the press and that newspapers are collected by future readers; they should be worthy of such association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose copy with some consciousness of character and future readership: avoid tawdry phrasing and ephemeral vulgarity if your notices may be preserved. Consider how present advertisements will be judged by posterity and collectors.
